sections.title: What is Stage Fright?
sections.content: Stage fright — also called performance anxiety — is your body's natural response to perceived threat. When you step in front of an audience, your brain activates the same fight-or-flight response triggered by physical danger. Your heart races, palms sweat, and your stomach knots up.
bullets: Stage fright is NOT a sign of weakness — it is a biological response
The same adrenaline that causes nerves also sharpens your focus
Every great speaker feels it; the difference is how they channel it

sections.title: Reframing Anxiety as Excitement
sections.content: Research from Harvard Business School shows that simply telling yourself 'I am excited' instead of 'I am nervous' dramatically improves performance. Both states feel identical in the body — racing heart, butterflies, heightened alertness. The only difference is how you label it.
bullets: Anxiety and excitement produce the same physiological arousal
Saying 'I am excited' repositions the energy as fuel, not friction
Practice this reframe every time you feel pre-speech jitters

sections.title: Adrenaline on a Roller Coaster
sections.content: Think about the last time you rode a roller coaster. Your heart pounded, your palms sweated, your breath quickened — the exact same sensations as stage fright. Yet on the coaster, you call it excitement. On stage, you call it fear. The body doesn't know the difference — your interpretation is everything.
sections.good: Before a speech: 'My heart is racing. This is my body getting ready to perform at my best.'
sections.bad: Before a speech: 'My heart is racing. Something is wrong. I'm going to mess up.'
sections.explanation: The same physical sensation produces completely different outcomes based on how you label it. Reframing turns anxiety into a performance-enhancing tool.

sections.instruction: When your palms sweat before a speech, what is your body actually doing?
options: Telling you that you are not ready
Preparing you for high performance by releasing adrenaline
Signaling that you should avoid the situation
sections.feedback: Palms sweating is a sign of adrenaline release — your body is preparing for peak performance, not warning you to flee.

sections.q: What is the most effective mental technique for managing stage fright?
options: Avoiding eye contact with the audience
sections.explain: Reframing anxiety as excitement leverages the identical physiological response and redirects it positively. Deep breathing helps, but reframing changes your mindset.

sections.statement: Great public speakers are born without stage fright — they never feel nervous.
sections.feedback: Every great speaker feels nervous. The difference is they have learned to channel that energy into their performance rather than fighting it.

sections.sentence: The technique of re-labeling nervousness as excitement is called {0} {1}.
sections.instruction: Fill in the two-word psychological term.
sections.feedback: Cognitive reframing means changing your interpretation of a sensation without changing the sensation itself.

questions.statement: Stage fright and excitement produce identical physical sensations in the body.
questions.feedback: Both trigger the same fight-or-flight response — racing heart, sweating, heightened alertness.

questions.q: Why does reframing anxiety as excitement improve performance?
options: It eliminates the physical symptoms entirely
It repositions nervous energy as fuel rather than friction
It tricks the audience into thinking you are confident
questions.feedback: Reframing doesn't change the physical response — it changes how you use that energy.
